title: CBS Midseason
body:
CBS has reshuffled its 2024‑25 midseason slate, pushing the tech‑savvy comedy “Cupertino” to a later debut, pairing the supernatural sitcom “Ghosts” with the new romantic comedy “Eternally Yours,” and expanding the flagship reality competition “Survivor” with a longer, 14‑episode run. The adjustments also see “Sheriff Country” and “FBI” slipping to later dates, signaling the network’s strategic gamble to balance fresh scripted fare with proven unscripted draws as it navigates a competitive broadcast landscape.

The most notable shift is the postponement of “Cupertino,” a workplace comedy set in the heart of Silicon Valley that was slated to launch in early January. CBS now plans to introduce the series in late February, giving the network extra breathing room to promote the show alongside “Ghosts” and “Eternally Yours.” Industry insiders suggest the delay is intended to avoid a crowded launch window that includes new offerings from streaming rivals and to allow the network to build momentum from the holiday ratings lull. By pairing the two comedies, CBS hopes to create a thematic block that captures both the quirky, supernatural humor of “Ghosts” and the modern romance of “Eternally Yours,” potentially drawing a broader audience than either could alone.

Meanwhile, the network’s procedural staples are experiencing a modest slide. “Sheriff Country,” a spin‑off of the long‑running “The Sheriff,” and the crime drama “FBI” will both premiere later in the spring schedule. The shift reflects CBS’s confidence that its core audience will remain loyal despite the later start, while also freeing up prime‑time slots for the network’s new scripted experiments. The move may also be a response to the modest ratings dip that “FBI” has seen in recent months, prompting executives to re‑tool its promotional push and pair it with stronger lead‑in programs.

In a bold departure from the trend of trimming reality‑TV formats, “Survivor” is set to return with a supersized season of 14 episodes, up from the typical 13‑episode order. The decision underscores the franchise’s enduring appeal and its ability to attract advertisers even as other long‑running reality series have been forced to shorten episodes or reduce the number of cycles per season. “Survivor” has consistently delivered strong live‑plus‑same‑day ratings, and the expanded run is expected to generate additional ad revenue and keep the show in the cultural conversation for a longer stretch of the year. The network also plans to air a special “All‑Stars” reunion episode, further capitalizing on the series’ loyal fan base.

Analysts view CBS’s midseason recalibration as a calculated effort to hedge its bets. The network is banking on the proven draw of “Survivor” to anchor viewership while giving its new scripted comedies the best possible launch conditions. The pairing of “Ghosts” and “Eternally Yours” could create a synergistic audience flow, especially if the shows share cross‑promotional tactics and guest appearances. At the same time, the delayed rollout of “Cupertino” may allow the series to benefit from a less fragmented promotional calendar, increasing its chances of breaking out in a crowded market.

Looking ahead, CBS’s revised schedule will be tested by audience response in the coming weeks. If “Survivor” sustains its ratings surge and the new comedies manage to capture enough buzz, the network could see a midseason ratings lift that offsets the earlier underperformance of its procedural lineup. Conversely, a lukewarm reception to the delayed comedies could prompt further schedule tweaks in the spring. Either way, CBS’s willingness to reshuffle its midseason slate highlights an industry increasingly focused on flexibility, data‑driven programming decisions, and the delicate balance between legacy franchises and fresh creative ventures.
